When you spear something, you drive something sharp and pointed into it — usually in one quick, forceful thrust. Think of a hunter pushing the tip of a spear weapon through a fish. That exact action — the sharp point going in, fast and direct — is what the verb captures.

The simplest one-line definition: to pierce or stab something with a sharp, pointed object (or in a sharp, pointed way).

Picture a fork going into a piece of food on your plate — that quick downward stab. That's spearing. The essential elements are:

  • Something pointed
  • A quick, direct motion
  • Penetrating into (or through) the target

Eating:

She speared a piece of chicken with her fork and lifted it to her mouth.

Here, the fork acts like a tiny spear. The sharp tines go into the food in one swift motion.

Fishing:

The fisherman stood knee-deep in the river and speared a trout.

A classic use — catching a fish by thrusting a pointed implement through it.

Gardening:

He walked around the park, spearing pieces of litter with a pointed stick.

Picking things up by stabbing them with a sharp stick.

Sports (especially wrestling or American football):

The wrestler speared his opponent — driving his shoulder into the man's stomach and slamming him to the ground.

Here, the person's body itself acts like a "spear." One powerful, direct charge into another person.

This is where the word becomes richer. "Spear" is often used to describe anything that feels sharp and sudden, even when no physical object is involved.

A piercing look:

His cold stare speared her from across the room.

The look felt sharp and direct, like it stabbed her — even though nothing physical happened.

A sudden feeling cutting through you:

A sharp pain speared through his chest.
Fear speared through her the moment she heard the news.
The icy wind speared right through his thin jacket.

In all these cases, something sharp, sudden, and intense "goes through" a person — whether it's pain, emotion, or cold air. The word captures that piercing, arrow-like quality.

"Spear" is a transitive verb — it always needs an object. You always spear something. You cannot just say "He speared" and stop there; that leaves the reader waiting. You must say what was speared:

✅ She speared the olive.
✅ He speared his rival.
❌ She speared. (incomplete — speared what?)

Forms:

  • Present: spear / spears → "He spears the fish effortlessly."
  • Past: speared → "She speared the olive."
  • Continuous: spearing → "He was busy spearing pieces of fruit."
  • Past participle: speared → "The fish had been speared."

These words are all in the same family, but each has its own personality:

Stab — implies violence, injury, or repeated thrusts, usually with a blade (a knife, a dagger). Spear is more neutral and can even be casual (spearing food at dinner).

Pierce — a broader, more general word. It just means making a hole through something. It doesn't suggest speed or force the way "spear" does.

Impale — the most extreme version. Something goes completely through a body or object, usually with deadly force. Impaling is severe; spearing can be as gentle as a fork in a salad.

Skewer — very close to spear, but skewer usually means threading something onto a long stick (like meat on a kebab skewer). The object ends up on the stick, not just stabbed once.

Jab — a quick, short thrust, but it doesn't always go deep or penetrate fully. A jab is more of a surface-level poke; a spear goes in.

Poke — the gentlest of all. No real penetration; just a light push with a finger or object.

• It is not slow or gradual. If something oozes or seeps in gently, you wouldn't use "spear."
  • It is not a cutting motion (that's slice, cut, slash).
  • It is not a blunt impact (that's hit, smash, knock). Spearing always involves a point.
  • It does not imply going back and forth (like sawing). It's one clean, forward motion.

To spear = to thrust something sharp and pointed into a target — quickly, directly, and in one motion. It's used literally (a fork in food, a harpoon in a fish, a tackle in sport) and figuratively (a glance that cuts, a pain that shoots through you, cold that knifes through clothing). The word always needs an object, and it always carries that sense of something pointed moving swiftly and decisively into something.
